extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism researchers, journalism students, and newsroom professionals interested in newsworthiness and editorial decision-making
extracted.subtask_short: newsworthiness coding with Deuze's five values
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Mark Deuze's five core occupational-ideology values as meta-level filters to select, evaluate, or code news stories for research or editorial decision-making. Usable for content analysis, newsworthiness prediction models, or newsroom policy guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Service
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists see themselves as providing a service to citizens of a democracy; stories matter because they help citizens understand their world and govern themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that contribute to public knowledge receive the 'newsworthy' label; trivial or purely entertainment stories are treated as lower-tier. For coding: look for public-interest framing, accountability emphasis, civic relevance indicators. Examples/anti-patterns: hard news and accountability stories accorded higher symbolic value; lifestyle/entertainment stories are demoted unless reframed to show civic/public-service relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity / Fairness / Impartiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists must be 'impartial, fair, and (therefore) trustworthy.' Stories must admit a balanced presentation to qualify as real journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that allow for balanced presentation or clearly mark different viewpoints are favored; one-sided stories require additional discursive labor or reframing and may be downgraded. For coding: record balance markers, presence of multiple viewpoints, neutrality of tone, and explicit efforts at fairness/verification. Outlets may emphasize this value differently (e.g., Reuters' focus on objectivity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists must be free of external influence (advertisers, governments, sources); editorial independence is a core value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories perceived as serving narrow interests (corporate PR, government propaganda) are demoted unless they are reframed to preserve editorial independence. For evaluation/coding: flag funding/advertising ties, source-dependence, indications of agenda-serving framing. Investigative outlets often emphasize autonomy; stories that appear to serve interested parties' agendas are suspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediacy / Speed / Actuality
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism's 'operational logic' requires reporting on breaking news and getting the story first; recency is itself a master criterion of newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recency/actuality receives a premium — stories age out of newsworthiness quickly, often within a single news cycle. For coding: include recency markers (timestamps, 'breaking' labels), front-page/breaking placement, and speed of publication. Trade-offs: immediacy can conflict with deeper public-service or ethical considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics / Social Responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists hold themselves to ethical standards (verification, harm minimization, source protection) and consider social responsibility in story selection and reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories must pass ethical filters to qualify as news; those obtained through ethically questionable means (privacy violations, deception) face higher hurdles to publication. For coding: note verification practices, disclosures about methods, protections for vulnerable subjects, and editorial ethical justifications. Outlets emphasizing investigative work may prioritize this value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalizable newsworthiness coding features
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of the five values can be operationalized and coded in stories via observable markers for use in content analysis or newsworthiness-prediction models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical features to code include: public-interest framing, balance markers, source-attribution markers, recency/timestamp markers, and ethical-disclosure markers. Use these as model features or manual coding categories. Also note implications: the five values are stable cross-nationally, predict brand differentiation by emphasis, and frequently conflict with audience-engagement (click-driven) metrics — code for such tensions where relevant.
